# The lamp that the Grey Point Trust would not replace — Transcript

https://harbor.example.org/e/2026-11-11

---

[00:00:00] Welcome back to Harbor Voices, the show about small ports and the people who keep them running.

[00:00:14] Today we are at Grey Point with Tobias Renn, who has kept the lighthouse there for 31 years.

[00:00:28] Thanks, Mara. The lamp still burns colza oil, about 23 litres a night in the winter months.

[00:00:42] How did the Grey Point Trust decide to keep the old lamp instead of fitting an electric one?

[00:00:56] The Grey Point Trust voted on it in March, and the old lamp won by 41 votes to nine.

[00:01:10] An electric lamp would have cost the Trust 145 thousand dollars before a single night of light.

[00:01:24] Tobias Renn keeps a ledger of every ship that passes, and the ledger is the reason we came.

[00:01:38] The first entry is from 1902, a coal barge called the Wren, and we have 221 volumes now.

[00:01:52] What does the ledger tell you about the harbour that the official port records do not?

[00:02:06] The port records count tonnage, but the ledger records weather, crews and who was late and why.

[00:02:20] Last winter the ledger showed 62 ships turning back at the bar, twice the number of the year before.

[00:02:34] The Harbour Board reportedly disputes that count and says its own radar logs show far fewer.

[00:02:48] It is unclear whose count is right, because the radar at North Quay was down for most of January.

[00:03:02] Why does it matter to a fishing family in the town whether the count is forty or eighty?

[00:03:16] Because the dredging budget follows the count, and the Harbour Board sets the dredging budget every spring.

[00:03:30] If the bar is not dredged, the larger boats of the Northwind Cooperative cannot land their catch here.

[00:03:44] The Northwind Cooperative lands about 71 percent of the fish sold at the Saturday market.

[00:03:58] I think the town forgets how much of its income crosses that bar in the dark every single night.

[00:04:12] Let us talk about the keeper's day, because people imagine it as lonely and quiet work.

[00:04:26] I trim the wick at dusk, wind the clockwork every four hours, and write the ledger before I sleep.

[00:04:40] The clockwork was built by Halden and Sons in 1911 and it has stopped only three times since then.

[00:04:54] Could a young person still learn this trade, or does the knowledge end with the keepers we have?

[00:05:08] Two apprentices started with the Trust this year, and one of them already reads the tide tables better than I do.

[00:05:22] The Grey Point Trust pays for the apprentices out of visitor tickets and a small grant from the county.

[00:05:36] We had 13400 visitors last summer, which is more than the lighthouse has ever seen in one season.

[00:05:50] Does the crowd change the place, and is there a point where the Trust would turn people away?

[00:06:04] We cap the tower at twelve people an hour, and nobody climbs after the lamp has been lit.

[00:06:18] There is a plan from the county to build a visitor centre on the meadow behind the keeper's cottage.

[00:06:32] I am against the visitor centre where it is drawn, because the meadow is where the terns nest in May.

[00:06:46] Supporters of the plan say the visitor centre would bring thirty jobs to a town that badly needs them.

[00:07:00] Both things are true, and I would rather see the centre built at North Quay beside the old customs shed.

[00:07:14] What would you ask the Harbour Board if you had five minutes in front of all its members?

[00:07:28] I would ask them to publish the radar logs, so that the town can compare them with the ledger.

[00:07:42] That is a fair request, and we will put the same question to the Harbour Board ourselves next week.

[00:07:56] Whatever they answer, the lamp will be lit at dusk, as it has been on every night since 1902.

[00:08:10] Tobias Renn, keeper of the Grey Point lighthouse, thank you for showing us the ledger and the lamp.

[00:08:24] Next time on Harbor Voices we visit the ice house at North Quay and the family that still runs it.
